    Template · 4 pages

    Data storytelling workbook

    Framing worksheets and a chart-choice decision tree.

    What is inside

    Framing worksheets and a chart-choice decision tree. The document is laid out to be printed, marked up, and handed across a table.

    • A one-page summary you can pin above a desk.
    • The full checklist, in the order we actually run it.
    • Three worked examples from student work.
    FormatTemplate
    Pages4
    SizeSample PDF
    UpdatedUpdated September 2026

    An accessible, readable alternative

    The workbook, right here.

    The same text as the downloadable PDF, available without a PDF reader.

    01 / Understand the task

    Framing worksheets and a chart-choice decision tree.

    Turn one small dataset into a defensible statement with an honest visual comparison.

    Choose one small, real example to work on. A focused attempt gives you better evidence than a general impression.

    Your example: ____________________________________________________________

    Your audience: ___________________________________________________________

    Your intended outcome: ___________________________________________________

    One constraint: __________________________________________________________

    02 / Put a method to work

    1. Write the decision the reader needs to make.

    2. Check units, missing values, source date and the population being described.

    3. Use bars for category comparisons, a line for change over time, or a table for exact lookup.

    4. Start comparable bar axes at zero and label the units.

    5. Write a title that states the finding without claiming more than the data supports.

    6. Add one limitation and a text alternative for the important relationship.

    Working notes: __________________________________________________________

    _________________________________________________________________________

    03 / A worked practice scenario

    Fictional attendance: January 24, February 30, March 27 learners.

    A line can show the sequence; a table makes the exact values easy to find. Do not describe the series as continuous growth.

    A fair summary: attendance peaked in February, then fell by three learners in March.

    Apply the method to your own example. What changes?

    Your first attempt: _______________________________________________________

    Your revision: ___________________________________________________________

    04 / Reflect and keep going

    Would the same conclusion remain fair if the reader inspected the raw numbers?

    What is clearer after using this workbook?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    What evidence supports that conclusion?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    What is the smallest useful next step?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    Feedback prompt: "I noticed ____. That helped / made it harder to ____. One thing to try is ____."

    You may adapt this original sample workbook for personal learning and classroom demonstrations.
